reminder: A finitely generated algebra is a quotient of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables.
definition: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) and $A$ a commutative $R$-[algebra](c:associative-algebra). Then $A$ is finitely generated over $R$ when a [surjective](c:surjection) [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism) $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]\to A$ of $R$-algebras exists, where $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is a [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring). Equivalently, $A\cong R[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I$ is a [quotient ring](c:quotient-ring) for some ideal $I$, so finitely many elements of $A$ give every element as a polynomial with coefficients in $R$.
examples: The polynomial ring $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is generated by $x_1,\dots,x_n$.
The ring $\mathbb Z[i]=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb Z$-algebra, and so is $k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3)$ over a field $k$.
Non-example: the polynomial ring $k[x_1,x_2,\dots]$ in infinitely many variables is not finitely generated over $k$, because finitely many polynomials involve only finitely many variables.
Non-example: $\mathbb Q$ is not a finitely generated $\mathbb Z$-algebra, because finitely many fractions lie in $\mathbb Z[1/N]$ for one integer $N$, and $\mathbb Z[1/N]\neq\mathbb Q$.

steps: Take a commutative ring $R$ and a finitely generated $R$-algebra $A$.
A quotient of a polynomial ring is a commutative ring with an $R$-action, so $A$ is an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) over $R$.
The special case adds one condition: finitely many elements of $A$ generate $A$ as an $R$-algebra.
links.why: General facts about algebras apply to a finitely generated algebra, and the extra condition gives control by finitely many generators.

reminder: In a first-countable space, every point has a countable neighbourhood base.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is first-countable when every [point](c:point) $x\in X$ has a [neighbourhood base](c:neighborhood-base) that is a [countable](c:countable-set) family $U_1,U_2,\dots$ of neighbourhoods. This means that every neighbourhood of $x$ contains some $U_n$. One can choose the $U_n$ nested, with $U_1\supseteq U_2\supseteq\cdots$.
examples: Every metric space is first-countable, because the open balls $B(x,1/n)$ form a neighbourhood base at $x$.
The space $\mathbb R^n$ is first-countable, and so is every second-countable space.

Non-example: an uncountable set with the cocountable topology is not first-countable, because countably many neighbourhoods of a point $x$ share another point $y$, and $X\setminus\{y\}$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ that contains none of them.

steps: Take a second-countable space $X$ with a countable base $\mathcal B$.
For a point $x$, the members of $\mathcal B$ that contain $x$ form a countable family.
Every neighbourhood of $x$ contains a member of $\mathcal B$ that contains $x$, so this family is a neighbourhood base at $x$.
Hence $X$ is first-countable, and the converse fails.
links.why: A fact proved for first-countable spaces, such as sequences deciding closure and continuity, holds in every second-countable space.

steps: Take a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$ with its metric topology and a point $x$.
The open balls $B(x,1/n)$ for $n\ge1$ form a countable family of neighbourhoods of $x$.
A neighbourhood of $x$ contains a ball $B(x,r)$, and $B(x,1/n)\subseteq B(x,r)$ when $1/n<r$.
So the balls form a countable neighbourhood base, and the metric topology is first-countable.
links.why: Sequences decide closure and continuity in every metric space, because metric spaces are first-countable.

reminder: The floor of a real number $x$ is the greatest integer that is at most $x$.
definition: The floor function is the [function](c:function) that sends a [real number](c:real-number) $x$ to the [integer](c:integer) $\lfloor x\rfloor$ with $\lfloor x\rfloor\le x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1$. This integer is unique, so $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is the greatest integer $n$ with $n\le x$, and $x-\lfloor x\rfloor$ lies in $[0,1)$.
examples: $\lfloor 2.7\rfloor=2$ and $\lfloor 5\rfloor=5$.
$\lfloor -1.2\rfloor=-2$, because $-2\le -1.2<-1$.
Non-example: truncation toward zero sends $-1.2$ to $-1$, so it is not the floor function on negative numbers.

reminder: A point is focal when the whole space is its only open neighbourhood.
definition: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space). A [point](c:point) $x\in X$ is focal when the only [open neighbourhood](c:open-neighbourhood) of $x$ is $X$ itself. Equivalently, every [open set](c:open-set) that contains $x$ equals $X$.
examples: In the Sierpinski space $\{0,1\}$ with open sets $\varnothing$, $\{1\}$ and $\{0,1\}$, the point $0$ is focal.
Every point of an indiscrete space is focal, because the only nonempty open set is the whole space.
Non-example: in the Sierpinski space the point $1$ is not focal, because $\{1\}$ is an open neighbourhood of $1$ that is smaller than the space.

reminder: A formal group is a group object in formal schemes, with its product given by power series.
definition: A formal group is a [group object](c:group-object) in a category of infinitesimal spaces, such as [formal schemes](c:formal-scheme) over a ring $R$. In dimension one, it is a formal group law: a [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) $F(X,Y)\in R[[X,Y]]$ with $F(X,0)=X$, $F(0,Y)=Y$ and $F(F(X,Y),Z)=F(X,F(Y,Z))$.
examples: The additive formal group law $F(X,Y)=X+Y$.
The multiplicative formal group law $F(X,Y)=X+Y+XY$, which comes from $(1+X)(1+Y)=1+F(X,Y)$.
Non-example: $F(X,Y)=X+Y+X^2$ is not a formal group law, because $F(X,0)=X+X^2\neq X$, so the unit law fails.

steps: Take a category with finite products, here the category of formal schemes over $R$.
A formal group is a [group object](c:group-object) in this category, with product, unit and inverse maps.
The special case adds that the underlying spaces are infinitesimal.
links.why: Every statement about group objects, such as the group laws as commuting diagrams, applies to formal groups.

steps: Take a [formal group law](c:formal-group-law) $F$ over a ring $R$.
Let $\widehat G$ be the formal scheme with coordinate ring $R[[X]]$.
Define the product $\widehat G\times\widehat G\to\widehat G$ by $(X,Y)\mapsto F(X,Y)$, with unit $X=0$.
Then $\widehat G$ is a formal group, so a formal group law is a formal group with a chosen coordinate.
links.why: A formal group law gives a concrete power series model of a one-dimensional formal group.

reminder: Maps out of a formally smooth algebra lift along every quotient by a nilpotent ideal.
definition: Let $A\to B$ be a [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism) of [commutative rings](c:commutative-ring), so $B$ is an $A$-[algebra](c:associative-algebra). Then $B$ is formally smooth over $A$ when, for every $A$-algebra $C$ and every [nilpotent ideal](c:nilpotent-ideal) $N$ of $C$, each $A$-algebra map $B\to C/N$ lifts to an $A$-algebra map $B\to C$. Here $C/N$ is a [quotient ring](c:quotient-ring).
examples: A polynomial ring $A[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is formally smooth over $A$, because a lift only needs lifts of the images of the variables.
A finite separable field extension $K/k$ is formally smooth, because Hensel-type lifting lifts every simple root of the minimal polynomial.

Non-example: the dual numbers $k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$ are not formally smooth over $k$, because the map $\varepsilon\mapsto t$ to $k[t]/(t^2)$ has no lift to $k[t]/(t^3)$, since a lift of $t$ has square $t^2\neq0$.

steps: Take a formally étale algebra $B$ over $A$.
By definition, every map $B\to C/N$ lifts to $C$ in exactly one way, for $N$ nilpotent.
In particular, every such map lifts at least once, so $B$ is formally smooth.
The étale case adds that the lift is unique.
links.why: A statement about lifting for formally smooth algebras applies to étale algebras, which are the formally smooth ones with unique lifts.

steps: Take a smooth $A$-algebra $B$ in the sense of algebraic geometry.
By definition, $B$ is formally smooth over $A$ and finitely presented as an $A$-algebra.
So $B$ has the lifting property of formal smoothness.
The smooth case adds the finite presentation condition.
links.why: Lifting arguments for formally smooth algebras apply to every smooth algebra.

reminder: The index of a Fredholm operator is the dimension of its kernel minus the dimension of its cokernel.
definition: Let $F:X\to Y$ be a [Fredholm operator](c:fredholm-operator), so its [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) and its [cokernel](c:cokernel) are [finite-dimensional](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space) vector spaces. The index of $F$ is the integer $\operatorname{ind}F=\dim\ker F-\dim\operatorname{coker}F$, where $\dim$ is the [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space). The index does not change when $F$ varies continuously among Fredholm operators.
examples: An invertible operator has kernel $0$ and cokernel $0$, so its index is $0$.
The right shift $S(x_1,x_2,\dots)=(0,x_1,x_2,\dots)$ on $\ell^2$ has kernel $0$ and a one-dimensional cokernel, so $\operatorname{ind}S=-1$.
Non-example: the zero operator on $\ell^2$ has an infinite-dimensional kernel, so it is not Fredholm and has no index.

steps: Take an [elliptic operator](c:elliptic-operator) $D$ on a compact manifold.
Between suitable Sobolev spaces, $D$ is a Fredholm operator.
Its analytical index is, by definition, the Fredholm index $\dim\ker D-\dim\operatorname{coker}D$.
links.why: An index theorem that computes an analytical index computes a Fredholm index of a concrete operator.

reminder: A Fredholm operator is a bounded linear map whose kernel and cokernel both have finite dimension.
definition: A [bounded linear operator](c:bounded-linear-operator) $T:X\to Y$ between [Banach spaces](c:banach-space) is Fredholm when its [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) is finite-dimensional and its [cokernel](c:cokernel) $Y/T(X)$ is finite-dimensional. In this case, the range $T(X)$ is automatically closed in $Y$, and the [finite-dimensional](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space) kernel and cokernel have an integer difference of dimensions, the index.
examples: Every invertible bounded operator is Fredholm, with kernel $0$ and cokernel $0$.
The operator $I+K$ with $K$ compact is Fredholm of index $0$.
Every linear map between finite-dimensional spaces is Fredholm.
Non-example: the zero operator on an infinite-dimensional Banach space has an infinite-dimensional kernel, so it is not Fredholm.

steps: Take a Fredholm operator $T:X\to Y$.
By definition, $T$ is a [bounded linear operator](c:bounded-linear-operator) between Banach spaces.
The special case adds that the kernel and the cokernel of $T$ are finite-dimensional.
links.why: All facts about bounded operators apply, and the finiteness condition makes the index defined.

reminder: A free resolution of a module is an exact chain of free modules that ends in the module.
definition: A free resolution of a [module](c:module) $M$ is an [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $\cdots\to F_2\to F_1\to F_0\to M\to0$ in which every $F_i$ is a [free module](c:free-module). Equivalently, it is a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $F_\bullet$ of free modules with a [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism) $F_\bullet\to M$, where $M$ sits in degree $0$.
examples: For $n\ge1$, the sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\,n\,}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/n\to0$ is a free resolution of $\mathbb Z/n$ over $\mathbb Z$.
Over $k[x,y]$, the Koszul complex $0\to k[x,y]\to k[x,y]^2\to k[x,y]\to k\to0$ is a free resolution of $k$.
Non-example: over $\mathbb Z/6$ the module $\mathbb Z/2$ is projective but not free, so the identity map $\mathbb Z/2\to\mathbb Z/2$ is a projective resolution that is not a free resolution.

steps: Take a free resolution $F_\bullet\to M$.
The map $F_\bullet\to M$ is a quasi-isomorphism, so $F_\bullet$ is a [homological resolution](c:homological-resolution) of $M$.
The free case chooses the class of free modules for the terms of the resolution.
links.why: General facts about resolutions apply, and freeness gives explicit bases for computing derived functors.

steps: Take a free resolution $F_\bullet\to M$ of a module $M$.
Every free module is projective, because a map out of it lifts along a surjection by choosing images of a basis.
So $F_\bullet\to M$ is an exact sequence of projective modules that ends in $M$.
Hence $M$ has a projective resolution, and the free case adds a basis in each term.
links.why: Every result proved with projective resolutions can use a free resolution.

reminder: The function field of an affine variety is the field of fractions of its ring of regular functions.
definition: Let $X$ be an [affine variety](c:affine-variety) over a [field](c:field) $k$, with ring of regular functions $\mathcal O(X)$. When $X$ is irreducible, $\mathcal O(X)$ is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain), and the function field $k(X)$ is its [field of fractions](c:field-of-fractions), the field of quotients $f/g$ with $g\neq0$.
examples: For the affine line $\mathbb A^1_k$, we have $\mathcal O=k[t]$, and $k(X)=k(t)$ is the field of rational functions.
For the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ over $\mathbb Q$, the function field is the field of fractions of $\mathbb Q[x,y]/(x^2+y^2-1)$, which is isomorphic to $\mathbb Q(t)$ through a rational parametrisation.
Non-example: $V(xy)\subset\mathbb A^2$ is reducible, and $k[x,y]/(xy)$ has zero divisors, so it has no field of fractions and no function field.

steps: Take an irreducible affine variety $X$ with ring of regular functions $\mathcal O(X)$.
Irreducibility makes $\mathcal O(X)$ an [integral domain](c:integral-domain).
So $\mathcal O(X)$ has a [field of fractions](c:field-of-fractions), built from quotients $f/g$ with $g\neq0$.
The function field is exactly this field of fractions.
links.why: Every fact about fraction fields applies, and the elements now have a geometric meaning as rational functions on $X$.

reminder: A fundamental matrix has as its columns a basis of solutions of a linear differential system.
definition: Consider a [linear differential system](c:linear-differential-equation) $x'=A(t)x$, where $A(t)$ is an $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) of continuous functions. A fundamental matrix is an $n\times n$ matrix function $\Phi(t)$ with $\Phi'(t)=A(t)\Phi(t)$ and $\det\Phi(t)\neq0$ for one (and hence every) $t$, so its columns are $n$ linearly independent solutions. The [determinant](c:determinant) condition says that these solutions form a basis of the solution space.
examples: For $x'=Ax$ with a constant matrix $A$, the matrix $e^{tA}$ is a fundamental matrix.
For $x'=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\,x$, the matrix $\Phi(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{t},e^{2t})$ is a fundamental matrix.
Non-example: for $x'=x$ in $\mathbb R^2$, the matrix with columns $(e^t,0)$ and $(2e^t,0)$ has determinant $0$, so its columns are dependent and it is not fundamental.

steps: Take a constant matrix $A$ and the system $x'=Ax$.
The matrix exponential $\Phi(t)=e^{tA}$ satisfies $\Phi'=A\Phi$ and $\Phi(0)=I$.
Also $\det e^{tA}=e^{t\operatorname{tr}A}\neq0$ for every $t$.
So $e^{tA}$ is a fundamental matrix, the constant-coefficient case with $\Phi(0)=I$.
links.why: Results on fundamental matrices, such as Floquet theory, reduce to the matrix exponential when the coefficients are constant.

reminder: Galois cohomology is the cohomology of a Galois group acting continuously on a discrete module.
definition: Let $G$ be a [profinite group](c:profinite-group), such as the absolute [Galois group](c:galois-group) of a field $K$, and let $M$ be a discrete $G$-[module](c:module) with a continuous action. The Galois cohomology groups $H^n(G,M)$ are the [group cohomology](c:group-cohomology) groups that one computes with continuous cochains $G^n\to M$.
examples: The group $H^0(G,M)=M^G$ is the group of invariants, and for a Galois extension $L/K$ with $G=\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ we get $H^0(G,L)=K$.
Hilbert's Theorem 90 says $H^1(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K),L^\times)=0$ for every finite Galois extension $L/K$.
The Brauer group of a field $K$ is $H^2(\operatorname{Gal}(K^{\mathrm{sep}}/K),(K^{\mathrm{sep}})^\times)$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z_p$ with its $p$-adic topology is a profinite module, not a discrete one, so this definition does not apply to it directly.

steps: Take a discrete module $M$ over a profinite group $G$.
Group cohomology uses all cochains $G^n\to M$ with the usual coboundary maps.
Galois cohomology uses only the continuous cochains, which are locally constant because $M$ is discrete.
For a finite group $G$, every cochain is continuous, so the two theories agree.
links.why: Tools of group cohomology, such as long exact sequences, work for Galois cohomology.

reminder: A geodesic circle is the set of points at a fixed small geodesic distance from a center.
definition: Let $M$ be a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of dimension $2$, let $p\in M$, and let $r$ be smaller than the injectivity radius at $p$. The geodesic circle of radius $r$ about $p$ is the image $\{\exp_p(rv)\}$ of the unit circle $\{v:|v|=1\}$ in the [tangent space](c:tangent-space) at $p$ under the [exponential map](c:exponential-map). It is the set of points at [geodesic](c:geodesic) distance $r$ from $p$.
examples: In the Euclidean plane, the geodesic circle of radius $r$ is the ordinary circle, of length $2\pi r$.
On the unit sphere, the geodesic circle of radius $r<\pi$ is the circle of latitude at angular distance $r$ from $p$, of length $2\pi\sin r$.
Non-example: on the unit sphere, $\{\exp_p(\pi v)\}$ is the single antipodal point, so radius $\pi$ gives no circle, because $r$ is not below the injectivity radius.

steps: Take the Euclidean plane, where geodesics are straight lines.
There $\exp_p(v)=p+v$, so the geodesic circle of radius $r$ is $\{p+rv:|v|=1\}$.
This set is the ordinary [circle](c:circle) of radius $r$ about $p$.
So the circle is the flat special case of a geodesic circle.
links.why: Geodesic circles let curvature enter circle formulas, since the length $2\pi r$ becomes $2\pi(r-Kr^3/6+\cdots)$.

reminder: A geometric morphism between toposes is an adjoint pair whose left adjoint preserves finite limits.
definition: A geometric morphism $f:\mathcal E\to\mathcal F$ between [toposes](c:topos) is a pair of [adjoint functors](c:adjoint-functor) $f^*\dashv f_*$, with $f^*:\mathcal F\to\mathcal E$ the inverse image and $f_*:\mathcal E\to\mathcal F$ the direct image. The left adjoint $f^*$ must preserve [finite limits](c:finite-limit).
examples: A continuous map $g:X\to Y$ gives a geometric morphism between the [sheaf](c:sheaf) toposes $\mathrm{Sh}(X)\to\mathrm{Sh}(Y)$, with $g^*$ the inverse image of sheaves and $g_*$ the direct image.
Every topos has a unique geometric morphism to $\mathbf{Set}$, with the constant-object functor as inverse image and global sections as direct image.
Non-example: for a set $A$ with two elements, the adjunction $A\times-\dashv(-)^A$ on $\mathbf{Set}$ is not a geometric morphism, because $A\times-$ does not preserve the terminal object.

steps: Take a geometric morphism $f$ with inverse image $f^*$ and direct image $f_*$.
By definition, $f^*$ is left adjoint to $f_*$.
So $f$ is an [adjunction](c:adjoint-functor) between two toposes.
The special case adds that the left adjoint preserves finite limits.
links.why: All facts about adjunctions apply to the pair $f^*\dashv f_*$, such as the preservation of colimits by $f^*$.

steps: Take a continuous map $g:X\to Y$ of topological spaces.
Pullback of sheaves gives a functor $g^*:\mathrm{Sh}(Y)\to\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ with right adjoint $g_*$.
The functor $g^*$ preserves finite limits, because the stalks of $g^*F$ are stalks of $F$.
So $g$ gives a geometric morphism of sheaf toposes.
links.why: Geometric morphisms extend continuous maps to toposes that have no points.

reminder: The golden ratio is the positive solution of $x^2=x+1$, about $1.618$.
definition: The golden ratio is the [real number](c:real-number) $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. It is the positive [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial) of the polynomial $x^2-x-1$, so $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$ and $1/\varphi=\varphi-1$.
examples: A rectangle with sides $\varphi$ and $1$ keeps its shape when one cuts off a unit square, because $1/(\varphi-1)=\varphi$.
The ratio $F_{n+1}/F_n$ of consecutive Fibonacci numbers tends to $\varphi$ as $n$ grows.
Non-example: the other root $\psi=(1-\sqrt5)/2\approx-0.618$ satisfies the same equation, but it is negative, so it is not the golden ratio.

reminder: The connectivity of a graph is the least number of vertices whose removal disconnects it.
definition: A [graph](c:graph) $G$ is $k$-connected when it has more than $k$ [vertices](c:vertex) and $G-S$ is [connected](c:connected-graph) for every set $S$ of fewer than $k$ vertices. The connectivity $\kappa(G)$ is the largest $k$ for which $G$ is $k$-connected.
examples: A cycle $C_n$ with $n\ge3$ is $2$-connected, because removing one vertex leaves a path, which is connected.
The complete graph $K_n$ is $(n-1)$-connected, and $\kappa(K_n)=n-1$.
The graph of a $d$-dimensional convex polytope is $d$-connected, by Balinski's theorem.
Non-example: the path $P_3$ is connected but not $2$-connected, because removing its middle vertex leaves two isolated vertices.

steps: Take $k=1$ in the definition of $k$-connected.
Then the only set $S$ with fewer than $1$ vertex is the empty set.
So $1$-connected says that $G$ has at least two vertices and is [connected](c:connected-graph).
Larger $k$ adds the demand that no small set of vertices disconnects $G$.
links.why: Connectivity measures how robustly a graph stays connected, and ordinary connectedness is its first level.

reminder: A graphical sequence is a list of numbers that are the vertex degrees of some simple graph.
definition: A finite sequence $d_1\ge d_2\ge\cdots\ge d_n$ of nonnegative integers is graphical when some simple [graph](c:graph) on $n$ [vertices](c:vertex) has [degrees](c:vertex-degree) $d_1,\dots,d_n$. A simple graph has no loops and no repeated edges. A graphical sequence has an even sum, and the Erdos-Gallai inequalities decide whether a sequence is graphical.
examples: The sequence $(2,2,2)$ is graphical, because the triangle has three vertices of degree $2$.
The sequence $(3,3,2,2)$ is graphical: take the complete graph $K_4$ and remove one edge.
Non-example: $(3,3,1,1)$ has an even sum but is not graphical, because two vertices of degree $3$ among four must both join every other vertex, which gives the other two vertices degree $2$.

reminder: The Gromov-Hausdorff distance of two compact metric spaces is the least Hausdorff distance over all joint isometric embeddings.
definition: For [compact metric spaces](c:compact-metric-space) $X$ and $Y$, the Gromov-Hausdorff distance $d_{GH}(X,Y)$ is the infimum of $d_H^Z(f(X),g(Y))$ over all [metric spaces](c:metric-space) $Z$ and all [isometric](c:isometry) embeddings $f:X\to Z$ and $g:Y\to Z$. Here $d_H^Z$ is the [Hausdorff distance](c:hausdorff-distance) in $Z$.
examples: If $X$ and $Y$ are isometric, then $d_{GH}(X,Y)=0$.
If $P$ is a point and $X$ is a compact metric space of diameter $D$, then $d_{GH}(P,X)=D/2$.
Non-example: the Hausdorff distance of two subsets of one fixed space $Z$ is not $d_{GH}$, because it depends on where the sets sit in $Z$ and it need not be $0$ for isometric copies.

reminder: A Grothendieck category is an abelian category with a generator, all coproducts and exact filtered colimits.
definition: A Grothendieck category is an [abelian category](c:abelian-category) $\mathcal A$ that has all small [coproducts](c:coproduct), in which the [filtered colimit](c:filtered-colimit) functor is an [exact functor](c:exact-functor), and which has a [generator](c:generator).
examples: The category of modules over any ring, such as the category $\mathbf{Ab}$ of abelian groups, is a Grothendieck category, and the ring itself is a generator.
The category of [abelian sheaves](c:abelian-sheaf) on a topological space is a Grothendieck category.
The category of quasi-coherent sheaves on a scheme is a Grothendieck category.
Non-example: the category of finite abelian groups is abelian but has no infinite coproducts, so it is not a Grothendieck category.

steps: Take a Grothendieck category $\mathcal A$.
By definition, $\mathcal A$ is an [abelian category](c:abelian-category).
The special case adds three conditions: all coproducts exist, filtered colimits are exact, and a generator exists.
links.why: Results on abelian categories apply, and the extra conditions give [enough injectives](c:enough-injectives).

steps: Take a ring $R$ and the [category of modules](c:mod) over $R$.
It is abelian, and its coproducts are direct sums.
Filtered colimits of modules are exact, because they are computed on underlying sets.
The module $R$ is a generator, because every module is a quotient of a free module.
links.why: Module categories are the model case, and the Gabriel-Popescu theorem says every Grothendieck category is close to one.

reminder: The Grothendieck construction glues the categories $F(c)$ of a functor $F$ into one category of pairs $(c,x)$.
definition: Let $F:C\to\mathbf{Cat}$ be a [functor](c:functor) from a [category](c:category) $C$ to the category [Cat](c:cat) of small categories. The Grothendieck construction $\int F$ has objects the pairs $(c,x)$ with $x$ an object of $F(c)$, and a morphism $(c,x)\to(c',x')$ is a pair $(f,\varphi)$ with $f:c\to c'$ in $C$ and $\varphi:F(f)(x)\to x'$ in $F(c')$. The projection $(c,x)\mapsto c$ makes $\int F$ a (op)[fibration](c:grothendieck-fibration) over $C$ with fibres $F(c)$.
examples: If $F$ is constant with value a category $D$, then $\int F$ is the product $C\times D$.
If $F:C\to\mathbf{Set}$ takes values in discrete categories, then $\int F$ is the category of elements of $F$.
For a group $G$ that acts on a set $X$, viewed as a functor $BG\to\mathbf{Set}$, the category $\int F$ is the [action groupoid](c:action-groupoid).
Non-example: the disjoint union $\coprod_c F(c)$ has the same objects but no morphisms between different fibres, so it is not $\int F$ unless $C$ is discrete.

steps: Take a group $G$ that acts on a set $X$.
View the action as a functor $F:BG\to\mathbf{Set}$ from the one-object category $BG$.
The category $\int F$ has objects $x\in X$ and a morphism $x\to x'$ for each $g$ with $gx=x'$.
That category is the [action groupoid](c:action-groupoid) of the action.
links.why: Facts about the Grothendieck construction apply to action groupoids and to categories of elements.

reminder: The commutator of two group elements $g$ and $h$ is $ghg^{-1}h^{-1}$, and it is trivial exactly when $g$ and $h$ commute.
definition: For an [ordered pair](c:ordered-pair) $(g,h)$ of [elements](c:element) of a [group](c:group) $G$, the commutator is $[g,h]=ghg^{-1}h^{-1}$. It equals the identity exactly when $gh=hg$. Some authors use $g^{-1}h^{-1}gh$ instead.
examples: In an abelian group, $[g,h]$ is the identity for all $g$ and $h$.
In the symmetric group $S_3$, with maps composed from right to left, $[(1\,2),(1\,3)]=(1\,2\,3)$.
Non-example: the conjugate $ghg^{-1}$ is not the commutator, because $[g,h]=(ghg^{-1})h^{-1}$ has the extra factor $h^{-1}$.

reminder: The group completion of a commutative monoid is the universal abelian group that receives a monoid map from it.
definition: The [forgetful functor](c:forgetful-functor) $U$ from [abelian groups](c:abelian-group) to [commutative monoids](c:add-comm-monoid) has a left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) $G$, called group completion. For a commutative monoid $M$, the group $G(M)$ comes with a monoid map $\eta:M\to G(M)$ with the [universal property](c:universal-property) that every monoid map from $M$ to an abelian group $A$ factors uniquely through $\eta$.
examples: The group completion of $(\mathbb N,+)$ is $(\mathbb Z,+)$, with the inclusion $\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$.
The group completion of the monoid $(\mathbb Z_{>0},\cdot)$ is the group $(\mathbb Q_{>0},\cdot)$.
The group completion of $(\{0,1\},\max)$ is the trivial group, because $a+a=a$ forces $\eta(a)=0$.

Non-example: the map $\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z/2$ with $n\mapsto n\bmod 2$ is not a group completion, because it is not universal: it factors through $\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$ but $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2$ does not factor back.

steps: Take the [forgetful functor](c:forgetful-functor) $U$ from abelian groups to commutative monoids.
Group completion $G$ is the left adjoint of $U$, by definition.
The unit $M\to UG(M)$ is the universal map from $M$ to an abelian group.
links.why: Facts about adjoints apply, such as group completion preserving colimits, because it is a left adjoint.

reminder: An H-space is a space with a continuous product that has a unit up to homotopy.
definition: An $H$-space is a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ with a [continuous](c:continuous-function) map $\mu:X\times X\to X$ and a [point](c:point) $e\in X$ such that the maps $\mu(e,-)$ and $\mu(-,e)$ are [homotopic](c:homotopy) to the identity of $X$. The product $\mu$ need not be associative, and the unit laws hold only up to homotopy.
examples: Every [topological group](c:topological-group) is an $H$-space, with its group product and its identity element.
The [loop space](c:loop-space) $\Omega X$ of a pointed space is an $H$-space under concatenation of loops, and the unit law holds only up to homotopy.
The sphere $S^7$ is an $H$-space through octonion multiplication, although it is not a group.
Non-example: the sphere $S^2$ is not an $H$-space, because among spheres only $S^0$, $S^1$, $S^3$ and $S^7$ are $H$-spaces.

steps: Take a topological group $G$ with continuous product $m$ and identity $e$.
The maps $m(e,-)$ and $m(-,e)$ equal the identity of $G$, so they are homotopic to it by a constant homotopy.
So $G$ is an $H$-space with $\mu=m$.
The converse fails, because an $H$-space needs neither strict associativity nor inverses.
links.why: Results on $H$-spaces apply to every topological group, which is the strict case.

steps: Take a pointed space $X$ and its [loop space](c:loop-space) $\Omega X$.
Define $\mu(\alpha,\beta)$ as the loop that runs $\alpha$ and then $\beta$.
The constant loop is a unit up to homotopy, by reparametrisation.
So $\Omega X$ is an $H$-space, and concatenation is associative only up to homotopy.
links.why: Loop spaces give a large supply of $H$-spaces that are not groups.

reminder: A Hamiltonian vector field is a vector field whose contraction with the symplectic form is the differential of a function.
definition: Let $(X,\omega)$ be a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold). A [vector field](c:vector-field) $v$ on $X$ is Hamiltonian when a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $H$ on $X$ exists with $\iota_v\omega=dH$, so the contraction of $v$ with the [differential form](c:differential-form) $\omega$ is exact. The function $H$ is a [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) of $v$, and the sign in $\iota_v\omega=\pm dH$ depends on the convention.
examples: On $\mathbb R^2$ with $\omega=dx\wedge dy$ and $H=(x^2+y^2)/2$, the vector field $v=y\,\partial_x-x\,\partial_y$ is Hamiltonian.
On $\mathbb R^{2n}$ with $\omega=\sum_i dq_i\wedge dp_i$, the Hamiltonian vector field of $H$ gives Hamilton's equations $\dot q_i=\partial H/\partial p_i$ and $\dot p_i=-\partial H/\partial q_i$.

Non-example: on the torus $\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ with $\omega=dx\wedge dy$, the field $\partial_x$ has $\iota\omega=dy$, which is closed but not exact, so the field is symplectic but not Hamiltonian.

steps: Take a Hamiltonian vector field $v$ with $\iota_v\omega=dH$.
Then $d(\iota_v\omega)=d(dH)=0$, so $\iota_v\omega$ is closed.
A [symplectic vector field](c:symplectic-vector-field) is one whose contraction with $\omega$ is closed.
So $v$ is symplectic, and the Hamiltonian case adds that the closed form is exact.
links.why: Every fact about symplectic vector fields, such as preserving $\omega$, holds for Hamiltonian ones.

reminder: A handle decomposition builds a manifold from balls by attaching handles one at a time.
definition: A handle decomposition of a compact [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ of dimension $n$ is a sequence $\varnothing=M_0\subset M_1\subset\cdots\subset M_m=M$ of $n$-dimensional submanifolds with boundary. Each $M_i$ comes from $M_{i-1}$ by attaching a $k$-handle, the product $D^k\times D^{n-k}$ of two [balls](c:ball), along $S^{k-1}\times D^{n-k}$ by an [embedding](c:embedding-of-differentiable-manifolds) into the boundary of $M_{i-1}$, after smoothing corners.
examples: The sphere $S^n$ has a handle decomposition with one $0$-handle and one $n$-handle.
The torus $T^2$ has a handle decomposition with one $0$-handle, two $1$-handles and one $2$-handle.
A Morse function on a closed manifold gives a handle decomposition with one $k$-handle for each critical point of index $k$.
Non-example: a CW structure on the torus lists open cells of different dimensions, but handles are $n$-dimensional pieces $D^k\times D^{n-k}$, so the cells alone are not handles.

reminder: A minimal Weierstrass equation has good reduction when its discriminant is a unit, so its reduction is an elliptic curve.
definition: Let $R$ be a [discrete valuation ring](c:discrete-valuation-ring) with fraction field $K$ and [residue field](c:residue-field) $k$, and let $W$ be a [Weierstrass curve](c:weierstrass-curve) over $K$ given by a minimal Weierstrass equation over $R$. Then $W$ has good reduction when its [discriminant](c:discriminant) $\Delta$ is a unit of $R$, that is, when $\Delta$ has absolute value $1$. Equivalently, the reduction of $W$ modulo the maximal ideal is an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) over $k$.
examples: Over $\mathbb Z_p$ with $p$ odd, the curve $y^2=x^3-x$ has $\Delta=64$, which is a unit, so it has good reduction at $p$.
The curve $y^2+y=x^3-x$ has discriminant $37$, so it has good reduction at every prime $p\ne37$.
Non-example: over $\mathbb Z_p$ with $p$ odd, the curve $y^2=x(x-1)(x-p)$ has $\Delta=16p^2(1-p)^2$, and its reduction $y^2=x^2(x-1)$ is singular, so the reduction is bad.

reminder: An object has an injective resolution when it is the start of an exact sequence of injective objects.
definition: An object $X$ of an [abelian category](c:abelian-category) has an injective resolution when an [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $0\to X\to I^0\to I^1\to I^2\to\cdots$ exists in which every $I^n$ is an [injective object](c:injective). Equivalently, $X$ has a [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism) into a [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) of injective objects in degrees $\ge0$.
examples: In abelian groups, the sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\to0$ is an injective resolution of $\mathbb Z$.
Every module over a ring has an injective resolution, because the category of modules has [enough injectives](c:enough-injectives).
Non-example: in the category of finitely generated abelian groups, $\mathbb Z$ has no injective resolution, because the only injective object there is $0$, so $\mathbb Z$ embeds in none.

steps: Take an object $X$ with an injective resolution $X\to I^\bullet$.
The map $X\to I^\bullet$ is a quasi-isomorphism, so $I^\bullet$ is a [resolution](c:resolution) of $X$.
The special case adds that every term $I^n$ is an injective object.
links.why: Injective terms make right derived functors computable from any such resolution.

reminder: An object has a projective resolution when it is the end of an exact sequence of projective objects.
definition: An object $X$ of an [abelian category](c:abelian-category) has a projective resolution when an [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $\cdots\to P_2\to P_1\to P_0\to X\to0$ exists in which every $P_i$ is [projective](c:projective). Equivalently, a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $P_\bullet$ of projective objects in degrees $\ge0$ has a [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism) $P_\bullet\to X$.
examples: In abelian groups, the sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\,n\,}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/n\to0$ is a projective resolution of $\mathbb Z/n$.
Every module has a projective resolution, because every module is a quotient of a free module and one can repeat this step on the kernel.
Non-example: in the category of finite abelian groups, $\mathbb Z/2$ has no projective resolution, because the only projective object there is $0$.

steps: Take an object $X$ with a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to X$.
The map $P_\bullet\to X$ is a quasi-isomorphism, so $P_\bullet$ is a [resolution](c:resolution) of $X$.
The special case adds that every term $P_i$ is projective.
links.why: Projective terms make left derived functors computable from any such resolution.

steps: Take a [free resolution](c:free-resolution) $F_\bullet\to M$ of a module $M$.
Each free module is projective, because maps out of it lift along surjections by choosing images of a basis.
So $F_\bullet\to M$ is an exact sequence of projective modules that ends in $M$.
Hence $M$ has a projective resolution, and free resolutions are the case with bases.
links.why: A result about projective resolutions applies to every free resolution.

reminder: In a Henselian ring, every simple root modulo the maximal ideal lifts to a root in the ring.
definition: A [local ring](c:local-ring) $(R,\mathfrak m)$ is Henselian when, for every [monic polynomial](c:monic-polynomial) $f\in R[x]$ and every element $\bar a$ of the [residue field](c:residue-field) $R/\mathfrak m$ with $\bar f(\bar a)=0$ and $\bar f'(\bar a)\neq0$, a root $a\in R$ of $f$ exists with $a\equiv\bar a$ modulo the [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak m$. This is the conclusion of Hensel's lemma, which holds for every [complete local ring](c:complete-local-ring).
examples: Every complete local ring is Henselian, for example $\mathbb Z_p$ and $k[[t]]$.
The ring of algebraic power series $k\{t\}$ is Henselian but not complete.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z_{(7)}$ is local but not Henselian, because $x^2-2$ has the simple root $3$ modulo $7$, while $2$ is not a square in $\mathbb Q$.

steps: Take a complete local ring $R$ and a monic $f\in R[x]$ with a simple root $\bar a$ modulo $\mathfrak m$.
Choose $a_0\in R$ that lifts $\bar a$, so $f(a_0)\in\mathfrak m$ and $f'(a_0)$ is a unit.
Newton's step $a_{n+1}=a_n-f(a_n)/f'(a_n)$ gives a Cauchy sequence in the $\mathfrak m$-adic topology.
Its limit is a root of $f$ that lifts $\bar a$, so $R$ is Henselian.
links.why: Results that need only Hensel lifting, such as the Artin approximation theorem, extend from complete rings to Henselian rings.

steps: Take a Henselian ring $R$.
By definition, $R$ is a [local ring](c:local-ring).
The special case adds a lifting property for simple roots of monic polynomials.
links.why: Every fact about local rings applies, and Hensel lifting gives extra tools for solving polynomial equations.

reminder: The Hilbert cube is the product of countably many unit intervals, a compact metrizable space.
definition: The Hilbert cube is the [product space](c:product-topology) $Q=[0,1]^{\mathbb N}$ of countably many copies of the [closed interval](c:closed-interval) $[0,1]$, with the product topology. It is [compact](c:compact-space) and [metrizable](c:metrizable-space), because the metric $d(x,y)=\sup_n2^{-n}|x_n-y_n|$ gives the product topology.
examples: A point of $Q$ is a sequence $(x_1,x_2,\dots)$ with every $x_n\in[0,1]$, and $Q$ is compact by Tychonoff's theorem.
Every separable metrizable space embeds in $Q$.
Non-example: the same set with the uniform metric $\sup_n|x_n-y_n|$ is not compact, because the sequences $e_k$ with a single $1$ at place $k$ are at distance $1$ from each other.

steps: Take the product topology on $Q=[0,1]^{\mathbb N}$.
Each factor $[0,1]$ is compact, so $Q$ is compact by Tychonoff's theorem.
The metric $d(x,y)=\sup_n2^{-n}|x_n-y_n|$ induces the product topology.
So $Q$ is a [compact metric space](c:compact-metric-space), and the special case adds that every separable metric space embeds in it.
links.why: Facts about compact metric spaces apply to $Q$, which serves as a universal model of separable metric spaces.

reminder: A Hurwitz polynomial has all its roots in the open left half of the complex plane.
definition: A [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p$ with real or complex coefficients is Hurwitz, or Hurwitz stable, when every [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial) $z\in\mathbb C$ of $p$ has $\operatorname{Re}z<0$, where $\mathbb C$ is the field of [complex numbers](c:complex-number). Equivalently, every solution of the equation $p(d/dt)y=0$ tends to $0$ as $t\to\infty$.
examples: The polynomials $s+1$ and $s^2+3s+2=(s+1)(s+2)$ are Hurwitz.
The polynomial $s^2+s+1$ has roots $(-1\pm i\sqrt3)/2$ with real part $-1/2$, so it is Hurwitz.
Non-example: $s^2+1$ has the roots $\pm i$ on the imaginary axis, whose real part is $0$, so it is not Hurwitz.

reminder: The hyperbolic plane is the complete simply connected surface of constant curvature $-1$.
definition: The hyperbolic plane is the [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of dimension $2$ that is [complete](c:complete-metric-space), [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) and has constant [Gaussian curvature](c:gaussian-curvature) $-1$, and it is unique up to isometry. In the upper half-plane model, it is $\{x+iy:y>0\}$ with the metric $(dx^2+dy^2)/y^2$.
examples: The upper half-plane with the metric $(dx^2+dy^2)/y^2$ is the hyperbolic plane, and its geodesics are vertical lines and semicircles centred on the real axis.
The Poincare disc, which is the unit disc with the metric $4(dx^2+dy^2)/(1-x^2-y^2)^2$, is the hyperbolic plane.
Non-example: the Euclidean plane has curvature $0$, so it is not hyperbolic, and a pseudosphere has curvature $-1$ but is not complete.

steps: Take the hyperbolic plane in the upper half-plane model.
The map $z\mapsto-1/z$ is an isometry that fixes $i$ and has differential $-\mathrm{id}$ there.
So the geodesic symmetry at $i$ is an isometry, and isometries move $i$ to every point.
Hence every point has such a symmetry, and the plane is a [symmetric space](c:symmetric-space).
links.why: Results on symmetric spaces apply to the hyperbolic plane, which is the simplest noncompact example.

reminder: The identity matrix has $1$ on the diagonal and $0$ elsewhere, so $IA=AI=A$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [ring](c:ring) with [identity element](c:identity-element) $1$. The identity matrix $I_n$ is the $n\times n$ [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix) over $R$ with every diagonal entry equal to $1$. It satisfies $I_nA=A$ and $AI_n=A$ for every $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ over $R$.
examples: The $2\times2$ identity matrix is $I_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
For a $2\times3$ matrix $A$, we have $I_2A=A=AI_3$.
Non-example: the $2\times2$ matrix with all entries $1$ is not an identity matrix, because it has nonzero entries off the diagonal and sends $(1,0)^T$ to $(1,1)^T$.

steps: Take the identity matrix $I_n$.
All its entries off the diagonal are $0$, so $I_n$ is a [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix).
The special case fixes every diagonal entry to be $1$.
links.why: Rules for diagonal matrices, such as multiplying entry by entry, apply to the identity matrix.

steps: Take the [matrix algebra](c:matrix-algebra) $M_n(R)$ with the matrix product.
For every $A$ in $M_n(R)$, we have $I_nA=AI_n=A$.
So $I_n$ is the [identity element](c:identity-element) of $M_n(R)$.
links.why: The identity matrix is the unit of the matrix ring, so all facts about identity elements apply to it.

reminder: In an impartial game, both players always have the same moves available from every position.
definition: An impartial game consists of a [set](c:set) $P$ of positions and, for each position $p$, a [subset](c:subset) $\mathrm{opt}(p)\subseteq P$ of options, with no infinite play. Two players move alternately by choosing an option of the current position, and under normal play the player who cannot move loses. Both players have the same options in every position.
examples: Nim is impartial: from a position with several heaps, either player may remove any positive number of objects from one heap.
Kayles is impartial, because both players may knock down the same pins.
Non-example: chess is not impartial, because White may move only white pieces and Black may move only black pieces.

steps: Take an impartial game with positions $P$ and options $\mathrm{opt}(p)$.
Its game tree has a node for each position and a child for each option.
Let the two players move at alternate nodes, and give the winner payoff $1$ and the loser payoff $-1$.
So the game is a two-player extensive-form game with perfect information and no chance moves, with equal moves for both players.
links.why: General facts about games in extensive form apply to impartial games.

reminder: An improper integral is a limit of ordinary integrals over intervals that grow toward an unbounded or singular end.
definition: Let $f$ be a [function](c:function) that is [Riemann integrable](c:riemann-integral) on every closed [interval](c:closed-interval) $[a,c]$ with $a\le c<b$, where $b$ is $\infty$ or a point at which $f$ is unbounded. The improper integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $\lim_{c\to b^-}\int_a^c f(x)\,dx$, and it converges when this limit exists and is finite. A bad left end, or a bad point inside the interval, is handled by splitting the integral at that point.
examples: $\int_1^\infty x^{-2}\,dx=\lim_{c\to\infty}(1-1/c)=1$.
$\int_1^\infty x^{-1}\,dx$ diverges, because $\int_1^c x^{-1}\,dx=\ln c\to\infty$.
Non-example: $\int_0^1 x^2\,dx$ is a proper integral, because the interval is bounded and the integrand is bounded, so no limit is needed.

steps: Take a bounded function $f$ that is [Riemann integrable](c:riemann-integral) on $[a,b]$.
The function $c\mapsto\int_a^cf$ is continuous on $[a,b]$.
So $\lim_{c\to b^-}\int_a^cf$ exists and equals $\int_a^bf$.
Hence the improper integral agrees with the Riemann integral whenever the Riemann integral exists.
links.why: Improper integrals extend the Riemann integral to unbounded intervals and unbounded functions without changing its value.

reminder: A nonzero module is indecomposable when it is not a direct sum of two nonzero submodules.
definition: A [module](c:module) $M$ over a ring $R$ is indecomposable when $M\neq0$ and $M\cong N_1\oplus N_2$ forces $N_1=0$ or $N_2=0$. Equivalently, $M$ is nonzero and is not the [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of two nonzero [submodules](c:submodule).
examples: The module $\mathbb Z$ is indecomposable over $\mathbb Z$, because two nonzero subgroups $a\mathbb Z$ and $b\mathbb Z$ always meet in $ab\mathbb Z\neq0$.
The module $\mathbb Z/p^n$ is indecomposable over $\mathbb Z$ for every prime $p$ and every $n\ge1$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z/6\cong\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/3$ splits into two nonzero submodules, so it is decomposable.

steps: Take a [simple module](c:is-simple-module) $S$, so $S\neq0$ and its only submodules are $0$ and $S$.
Suppose $S=N_1\oplus N_2$ for two submodules $N_1$ and $N_2$.
Each $N_i$ is $0$ or $S$, and $N_1\cap N_2=0$, so one of them is $0$.
So $S$ is indecomposable, and the converse fails, as $\mathbb Z$ shows.
links.why: Results on indecomposable modules, such as the Krull-Schmidt theorem, cover simple modules as the smallest case.

reminder: An initial value problem asks for a solution of a differential equation that takes given values at a starting point.
definition: An initial value problem is a differential equation together with initial data. For an [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $y^{(m)}=F(t,y,\dots,y^{(m-1)})$, the data are the values of $y,\dots,y^{(m-1)}$ at one time $t_0$. For a [partial differential equation](c:partial-differential-equation), the data are values of the unknown [function](c:function) and its normal derivatives on a hypersurface, and a solution must satisfy both the equation and the data.
examples: The problem $y'=y$ with $y(0)=1$ has the unique solution $y=e^t$.
The wave equation $u_{tt}=u_{xx}$ with $u(x,0)=g(x)$ and $u_t(x,0)=h(x)$ is an initial value problem, and d'Alembert's formula solves it.
Non-example: $y''+y=0$ with $y(0)=0$ and $y(\pi)=0$ gives values at two points, so it is a boundary value problem, and it has infinitely many solutions $c\sin t$.

reminder: An inner function is a bounded holomorphic function on the unit disc whose boundary values have modulus $1$ almost everywhere.
definition: An inner function is a bounded [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f$ on the [unit disc](c:unit-disc) $\mathbb D$ whose radial limits $f(e^{i\theta})=\lim_{r\to1^-}f(re^{i\theta})$ satisfy $|f(e^{i\theta})|=1$ for almost every $\theta$. Such a function lies in the [Hardy space](c:hardy-space) $H^\infty$ and has $|f|\le1$ on $\mathbb D$.
examples: The function $f(z)=z^n$ is inner, because $|f|=1$ on the whole circle.
A finite Blaschke product $\prod_k\frac{z-a_k}{1-\bar a_kz}$ with every $|a_k|<1$ is inner.
The singular inner function $\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{1+z}{1-z}\big)$ is inner and has no zeros.
Non-example: $f(z)=(1+z)/2$ is bounded and holomorphic, but $|f(e^{i\theta})|=|\cos(\theta/2)|<1$ for almost every $\theta$, so it is not inner.

reminder: An inscribed angle has its vertex on a circle and its two sides are chords of the circle.
definition: An inscribed angle in a [circle](c:circle) is an [angle](c:angle) whose vertex lies on the circle and whose two sides contain [chords](c:chord) of the circle. Its measure is half the measure of the central angle that subtends the same arc.
examples: An angle inscribed in a semicircle, which subtends a diameter, is a right angle.
All inscribed angles that subtend the same arc from the same side are equal.
Non-example: an angle formed by two crossing chords has its vertex inside the circle, so it is not an inscribed angle.

reminder: The intersection multiplicity at a point counts how many times two subvarieties meet there.
definition: Let $V$ and $W$ be subvarieties of a smooth [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) $X$ that meet at an isolated point $p$, with $\dim V+\dim W=\dim X$. The intersection multiplicity at $p$ is $\sum_{i\ge0}(-1)^i\,\ell\big(\operatorname{Tor}_i^{\mathcal O_{X,p}}(\mathcal O_{V,p},\mathcal O_{W,p})\big)$, where $\ell$ is the [length](c:length-of-an-object) over the [local ring](c:local-ring) $\mathcal O_{X,p}$. When $V$ and $W$ are Cohen-Macaulay at $p$, it is the length of $\mathcal O_{X,p}/(I_V+I_W)$.
examples: Two lines in $\mathbb A^2$ that cross at a point have intersection multiplicity $1$ there.
The parabola $y=x^2$ and the line $y=0$ meet at the origin with multiplicity $2$, because $k[x,y]_{(x,y)}/(y,y-x^2)\cong k[x]_{(x)}/(x^2)$ has length $2$.
By Bezout's theorem, two projective plane curves of degrees $m$ and $n$ without a common component have multiplicities that add up to $mn$ over an algebraically closed field.
Non-example: two equal lines in $\mathbb A^2$ meet along a whole line and not at an isolated point, so this multiplicity is not defined for them.

reminder: A measure is invariant when every transformation in the group or monoid preserves the measure of every measurable set.
definition: Let a [monoid](c:monoid) $G$, for example a group, act by [measurable](c:measurable-function) maps $T_g:X\to X$ on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $X$, which is a [group action](c:group-action) in the case of a group. A [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ on $X$ is invariant when $\mu(T_g^{-1}(A))=\mu(A)$ for every $g\in G$ and every measurable set $A$.
examples: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is invariant under all translations.
Lebesgue measure on $[0,1)$ is invariant under the doubling map $T(x)=2x\bmod1$, because $T^{-1}(A)$ has the same total length as $A$.
Non-example: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ is not invariant under $x\mapsto2x$, because $\lambda(T^{-1}[0,1])=\lambda([0,1/2])=1/2\neq1$.

steps: Take a locally compact group $G$ that acts on itself by left translation $T_g(x)=gx$.
A left [Haar measure](c:haar-measure) $\mu$ satisfies $\mu(gA)=\mu(A)$ for all $g$ and all measurable $A$.
Since $T_g^{-1}(A)=g^{-1}A$, this says that $\mu$ is invariant under the action.
So a Haar measure is an invariant measure for the action of $G$ on itself.
links.why: Results on invariant measures, such as the ergodic decomposition, apply to Haar measure.

reminder: In an inverse semigroup, every element $s$ has exactly one $t$ with $sts=s$ and $tst=t$.
definition: An inverse semigroup is a [semigroup](c:semigroup) $S$ in which every [element](c:element) $s$ has exactly one [inverse](c:inverse) $s^{-1}\in S$ with $ss^{-1}s=s$ and $s^{-1}ss^{-1}=s^{-1}$. Equivalently, every element has at least one such partner, and the idempotents of $S$ commute.
examples: Every group is an inverse semigroup, and $s^{-1}$ is the usual inverse.
A semilattice, which is a commutative semigroup of idempotents, is an inverse semigroup with $s^{-1}=s$.
The symmetric inverse monoid of all [partial bijections](c:partial-bijection) of a set is an inverse semigroup.
Non-example: on $\{a,b\}$ with the product $xy=x$ and $s=a$, both $t=a$ and $t=b$ satisfy $sts=s$ and $tst=t$, so inverses are not unique.

steps: Take a [group](c:group) $G$ as a semigroup under its product.
For $s\in G$, the group inverse $s^{-1}$ satisfies $ss^{-1}s=s$ and $s^{-1}ss^{-1}=s^{-1}$.
It is the only such element, because $sts=s$ gives $t=s^{-1}$ after multiplying by $s^{-1}$.
So $G$ is an inverse semigroup whose only idempotent is the identity.
links.why: Results on inverse semigroups apply to groups, which are the inverse semigroups with one idempotent.

steps: Take an inverse semigroup $S$.
It is a [semigroup](c:semigroup), because its product is associative.
The special case adds a unique partner $s^{-1}$ for each $s$ with $ss^{-1}s=s$ and $s^{-1}ss^{-1}=s^{-1}$.
links.why: General facts about semigroups apply, and the extra structure makes $S$ act like a semigroup of partial symmetries.

reminder: An involution is a map that equals its own inverse, so applying it twice gives the identity.
definition: An involution is a [function](c:function) $f:X\to X$ with $f\circ f=\mathrm{id}_X$. Then $f$ is its own [inverse function](c:inverse-function), so $f$ is a bijection.
examples: Negation $x\mapsto-x$ on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$ are involutions.
The transpose of matrices and the complement of subsets of a set are involutions.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x+1$ on $\mathbb Z$ is not an involution, because applying it twice gives $x\mapsto x+2$, and a rotation of the plane by $90^\circ$ fails in the same way.

steps: Take an involution $f:X\to X$ with $f\circ f=\mathrm{id}$.
Then $f$ is a two-sided inverse of itself, so $f$ is a [bijection](c:bijection).
The special case adds that the inverse of $f$ is $f$ itself.
links.why: Every fact about bijections applies, and the involution splits its set into fixed points and two-element orbits.

steps: Take a hyperplane through the origin of $\mathbb R^m$ with unit normal $n$, and its reflection $s(x)=x-2\langle x,n\rangle n$.
Then $\langle s(x),n\rangle=-\langle x,n\rangle$.
So $s(s(x))=s(x)+2\langle x,n\rangle n=x$.
Hence every [reflection](c:reflection-at-a-hyperplane) is an involution.
links.why: Reflections are the model involutions, so facts about involutions apply to them.

reminder: A group is perfect when it equals its own commutator subgroup.
definition: A [group](c:group) $G$ is perfect when $G=[G,G]$, where $[G,G]$ is the [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup) generated by all [commutators](c:group-commutator) $ghg^{-1}h^{-1}$. Equivalently, the [abelianization](c:abelianization) $G/[G,G]$ is the [trivial group](c:trivial-group), so every element of $G$ is a product of commutators.
examples: The trivial group is perfect, and so is the alternating group $A_n$ for $n\ge5$.
The group $SL_2(\mathbb R)$ is perfect.
Non-example: $S_3$ is not perfect, because its commutator subgroup is $A_3\neq S_3$, and every nontrivial abelian group has $[G,G]=1\neq G$.

reminder: A field is real closed when $-1$ is not a sum of squares, $x$ or $-x$ is a square, and odd-degree polynomials have roots.
definition: A [field](c:field) $R$ is real closed when three conditions hold. First, $R$ is [formally real](c:formally-real-field), so $-1$ is not a sum of squares in $R$. Second, for every $x\in R$ one of $x$ and $-x$ is a square. Third, every [polynomial](c:polynomial) of odd degree over $R$ has a [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial) in $R$.
examples: The field $\mathbb R$ of [real numbers](c:real-number) is real closed.
The field of real algebraic numbers is real closed.
Non-example: $\mathbb Q$ is formally real but not real closed, because neither $2$ nor $-2$ is a square in $\mathbb Q$.
Non-example: $\mathbb C$ is not real closed, because $-1=i^2$ is a square.

steps: Take a real closed field $R$.
The first condition says that $-1$ is not a sum of squares in $R$.
So $R$ is a [formally real field](c:formally-real-field).
The special case adds the square condition and the odd-degree root condition.
links.why: Facts about formally real fields apply, and the extra conditions fix a unique ordering of the field.

steps: Take the field of [real numbers](c:real-number) with its usual order.
Every sum of squares is nonnegative, so $-1$ is not a sum of squares.
For each $x$, the nonnegative one of $x$ and $-x$ has a real square root.
An odd-degree real polynomial changes sign, so it has a root by the intermediate value theorem.
links.why: The real numbers meet all three conditions, so statements proved for every real closed field, such as quantifier elimination, hold for them.

reminder: A root system is a root pairing whose roots span the root space and whose coroots span the coroot space.
definition: A [root pairing](c:root-pairing) has [modules](c:module) $M$ and $N$ with a perfect [pairing](c:pairing) $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:M\times N\to R$, roots $\alpha_i\in M$ and coroots $\alpha_i^\vee\in N$ with $\langle\alpha_i,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle=2$, such that every reflection $x\mapsto x-\langle x,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\alpha_i$ permutes the roots, and dually the coroots. It is a root system when the roots span $M$ and the coroots span $N$.
examples: The roots $\pm\alpha$ in $\mathbb R$, with coroots $\pm\alpha^\vee$, form the root system $A_1$.
The six roots of $A_2$ in the plane, at angles of $60^\circ$ to each other, form a root system.
Non-example: in $M=N=\mathbb R^2$, the roots $\pm e_1$ with coroots $\pm2e_1$ form a root pairing, but the roots span only a line, so it is not a root system.

steps: Take a root system, given by modules $M$ and $N$ with roots and coroots that span them.
Forgetting the two spanning conditions leaves a [root pairing](c:root-pairing).
So every root system is a root pairing, and the special case adds that the roots span $M$ and the coroots span $N$.
links.why: Facts about root pairings apply, and the spanning conditions let the roots describe the whole ambient space.

reminder: A module is semisimple when every submodule has a complement.
definition: A [module](c:module) $M$ is semisimple when every [submodule](c:submodule) $N$ has a complement, which is a submodule $N'$ with $M=N\oplus N'$. Equivalently, $M$ is a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of [simple modules](c:is-simple-module).
examples: Every vector space is a semisimple module over its field, because it is a direct sum of copies of the field.
The $\mathbb Z$-module $\mathbb Z/6\cong\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/3$ is semisimple.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z$ is not a semisimple $\mathbb Z$-module, because the submodule $2\mathbb Z$ has no complement.

steps: Take a [simple module](c:is-simple-module) $S$ with only the submodules $0$ and $S$.
A submodule $N$ is $0$ or $S$, and its complement is $S$ or $0$.
So every submodule of $S$ has a complement, and $S$ is semisimple.
A general semisimple module is a direct sum of such simple modules.
links.why: Results on semisimple modules cover simple modules as the case with one summand.

reminder: A ring of sets is a family of sets that contains the empty set and is closed under union and difference.
definition: A ring of sets on a [set](c:set) $X$ is a family $\mathcal C$ of [subsets](c:subset) of $X$ with $\varnothing\in\mathcal C$ such that $A\cup B\in\mathcal C$ and $A\setminus B\in\mathcal C$ whenever $A,B\in\mathcal C$. Then $\mathcal C$ is also closed under intersection, because $A\cap B=A\setminus(A\setminus B)$.
examples: The finite subsets of any set $X$ form a ring of sets.
The finite unions of half-open intervals $[a,b)$ in $\mathbb R$ form a ring of sets.
The power set of any set is a ring of sets.
Non-example: the open subsets of $\mathbb R$ are closed under union but not under difference, because $(0,2)\setminus(1,3)=(0,1]$ is not open.

steps: Take a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\mathcal A$ on $X$.
It contains $\varnothing$, which is the complement of $X$.
It is closed under finite unions, and under difference because $A\setminus B=(A^c\cup B)^c$.
So $\mathcal A$ is a ring of sets, and the sigma-algebra adds $X\in\mathcal A$ and countable unions.
links.why: Results about rings of sets, such as extension of measures, apply to every sigma-algebra.

steps: Take a ring of sets $\mathcal C$.
It contains $\varnothing$ and is closed under intersection.
For $A,B\in\mathcal C$, the difference $A\setminus B$ is one member of $\mathcal C$, so it is a finite disjoint union of members.
So $\mathcal C$ is a [semiring of sets](c:is-set-semiring), and the ring adds closure under union and difference.
links.why: Facts about semirings of sets apply to rings of sets.

reminder: A module is simple when it has exactly two submodules, the zero module and the whole module.
definition: A [module](c:module) $M$ is simple when it has exactly two [submodules](c:submodule), $0$ and $M$. So $M\neq0$, and every nonzero element of $M$ generates $M$.
examples: A field $k$ is a simple module over itself, and so is every one-dimensional vector space.
The group $\mathbb Z/p$ is a simple $\mathbb Z$-module for each prime $p$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z/6$ is not simple over $\mathbb Z$, because $2\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ is a submodule strictly between $0$ and the module.

steps: Take a simple module $S$ in the category of modules over a ring.
The subobjects of $S$ in this category are exactly the submodules of $S$.
So $S$ is nonzero and has only the zero subobject and itself as subobjects.
Hence $S$ is a [simple object](c:simple) of the module category.
links.why: Results on simple objects, such as Schur's lemma, apply to simple modules.

reminder: An $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple $(h,e,f)$ has $h\neq0$, $[e,f]=h$, $[h,e]=2e$ and $[h,f]=-2f$.
definition: In a [Lie ring](c:lie-ring) $L$, an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple is a triple $(h,e,f)$ of elements with $h\neq0$, $[e,f]=h$, $[h,e]=2e$ and $[h,f]=-2f$, where $[\cdot,\cdot]$ is the [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket). These are the relations of the standard basis of the [special linear Lie algebra](c:special-linear-lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, so the subalgebra that the triple generates is a copy of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$.
examples: In $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$, the matrices $h=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, $e=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $f=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ form an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple.
If $(h,e,f)$ is an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple, then so is $(-h,f,e)$.
Non-example: $(0,0,0)$ satisfies the bracket relations, but $h=0$, which the definition forbids.
